questions.q: What is the only thing a computer's processor understands directly?
questions.explain: The processor runs machine code. You write source code, which people can read, and another program turns it into something the processor can do.
options: JavaScript source code
Machine code: long lists of numbers, each a tiny instruction
English sentences
Any text saved in a .js file

questions.q: In the lesson's first program, each line console.log("…"); is called a…
questions.explain: A program is made of statements, instructions that run one after another. By default they run from top to bottom.
options: compiler
statement: one instruction
runtime
package

questions.q: What does a compiler do?
questions.explain: A compiler works ahead of time, like translating a whole book and then printing it. An interpreter carries out the code while it runs, like translating as people speak.
options: Reads the source code and carries it out line by line while the program runs
Translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and saves the result as a new file
Checks that the code has no logic errors
Downloads the packages a project needs

questions.q: What is an interpreter good at, compared with a compiler?
questions.explain: An interpreter can start at once, so you edit and rerun without building first. Compiled programs are usually faster once they run.
options: Making the fastest possible programs
Starting quickly, and changing code without a build step
Finding logic errors automatically
Running without any runtime

questions.q: Which of these languages is usually compiled ahead of time?
questions.explain: C, C++, Go and Rust are compiled before they run. Python, Ruby and early JavaScript were run by interpreters.
options: Python
Ruby
Go
Early JavaScript

questions.q: How do modern JavaScript engines use JIT ("just in time") compilation?
questions.explain: JIT gives both a quick start and fast code. The engine watches which parts run again and again and compiles those in the background. You never run a compiler yourself.
options: You must run a compiler yourself before every node command
They compile the whole file to a new file before starting
They start running at once with an interpreter, then compile the "hot" code that runs often to fast machine code
They never compile anything; they only interpret

questions.q: What is the runtime?
questions.explain: The engine only runs the language. The runtime adds the extra tools around it. console.log is one of them: the runtime gives it to your code.
options: The time a program takes to finish
Another name for the JavaScript engine alone
The whole environment a program runs in: the engine plus tools to print, read files, use the network and wait for timers
The list of packages a project depends on

questions.q: How does TypeScript code run?
questions.explain: TypeScript adds a compile step back: the TypeScript compiler produces plain JavaScript, which the engine runs like any other JavaScript.
options: V8 runs TypeScript directly, with no extra step
A compiler turns it into JavaScript, and that JavaScript then runs as usual
It is interpreted by the browser's Network tab
It is turned into Java first

questions.q: Which JavaScript engine is inside Node.js?
questions.explain: Node.js is V8, Google's engine (also used in Chrome and Edge), plus the tools a server needs. SpiderMonkey is Firefox's engine, JavaScriptCore is Safari's, and ECMAScript is the standard they all follow.
options: SpiderMonkey
JavaScriptCore
V8
ECMAScript

questions.q: Why does the same JavaScript run in Chrome, Firefox and Safari, even though they use different engines?
questions.explain: V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore are different programs, but they all follow the ECMAScript standard. That standard defines what JavaScript code means.
options: Because they all use V8
Because all the engines follow the same standard, ECMAScript
Because JavaScript is compiled to Java first
Because Node.js is installed in every browser

questions.q: What does node -p process.versions.v8 do?
questions.explain: node -p runs one expression and prints its result. Here that is the version of V8 your Node.js contains, which depends on your Node.js version.
options: Installs a new version of V8
Runs one expression and prints the result: the V8 version inside your Node.js
Prints the path of the node program
Starts a web server on port 8

questions.q: Which of these is available to JavaScript in the browser, but not in Node.js?
questions.explain: The browser runtime gives you the page (document) and window. Node.js has no page, but has process, files and network servers. console.log and Math exist in both.
options: process
document, the web page
console.log
Math

questions.q: A sign-up page checks in the browser that the password is long enough. Is that enough?
questions.explain: Any code sent to the browser can be read and changed by the visitor. A check in the page is a convenience for the user; the real check always happens on the server.
options: Yes, the browser check stops every bad request
Yes, if the check is written in JavaScript
No, the server must check again: the visitor controls the browser and can change or skip its code
No, the check should be removed from the page completely

questions.q: Who controls JavaScript that runs on your Node.js server?
questions.explain: Server code stays on your server, so visitors cannot read or change it. Browser code is sent to the visitor, who can do anything with it.
options: The visitor who sends the request
You: the code stays on your server
Whoever uses the Chrome browser
Nobody, it runs on its own

questions.q: How are Java and JavaScript related?
questions.explain: They were made by different people and work differently. Java must be compiled and wants the type of every variable. JavaScript runs from the source and does not ask for types.
options: JavaScript is the newer version of Java
JavaScript is Java that runs in a browser
They are different languages; the names are alike only for marketing reasons from 1995
Java is the compiled version of JavaScript

questions.q: Is your file order.js an executable program?
questions.explain: node (or node.exe) is the executable: the operating system can start it directly. Your .js file is source text that Node.js reads and runs.
options: Yes, you can double-click it to run it
No, it is text; you run it by giving it to Node.js with node order.js
Yes, because it ends in .js
No, it must first be uploaded to npm

questions.q: Which sentence describes the difference between a library and a framework?
questions.explain: With a library, you decide what to call and when. A framework is in charge: you hand it your pieces, and it decides when they run. ZudoJS works this way.
options: A library is free; a framework costs money
You call a library; a framework calls you
A library is written in JavaScript; a framework is written in TypeScript
A library runs in the browser; a framework runs on the server

questions.q: Your project needs the package @zudojs/errors. What is that package to your project?
questions.explain: A package is published code with a name and a version. The packages your project needs are its dependencies, listed in package.json.
options: A runtime
A dependency
An engine
A syntax error

questions.q: In package.json, what does the line "@zudojs/schema": "^1.1.1" under dependencies say?
questions.explain: Each line under dependencies is a package name and the versions the project accepts. npm is where these packages are published.
options: The project was written by the author @zudojs
The project needs the package @zudojs/schema, in the versions it accepts
The file schema.js is on line 1
The project is version 1.1.1

questions.q: A file has a missing ) on line 5. What happens to lines 1 to 4 when you run it?
questions.explain: The engine reads the whole file before running it. If the grammar is broken anywhere, nothing runs at all, not even the lines before the mistake.
options: They run, and the program stops at line 5
They do not run: the whole file is rejected before anything runs
They run, and line 5 is skipped
They run twice

questions.q: A program prints three lines, then stops with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined. What kind of error is it?
questions.explain: The grammar was fine, so the first lines ran. Then one statement could not be carried out and the program stopped. That is a runtime error. A syntax error would print nothing.
options: A syntax error
A runtime error
A logic error
A compiler error

questions.q: A shop's total shows 5 when it should show 50, and there is no error message. What kind of mistake is this, and how do you catch it?
questions.explain: Logic errors print no message: the code runs but computes the wrong thing. You only find them by comparing the real output with the expected one, which is what tests do.
options: A syntax error; read the error message
A runtime error; add more console.log lines until it crashes
A logic error; check the output against what you expected, for example with tests
No mistake; the engine rounds totals on purpose

questions.q: Node.js prints broken.js:2, the line, a row of ^, and SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list, then lines starting with at. What should you read first?
questions.explain: Read from the top. The file name and line tell you where, the ^ marks the place, and the message tells you what is wrong. For a syntax error, the at lines are Node.js's own internals.
options: The at lines at the bottom, which are Node.js internals
The top: the file and line number, the marked place, and the error message
Only the Node.js version at the end
Nothing, syntax errors cannot be read

questions.q: What is a stack trace?
questions.explain: After a runtime error, the stack trace shows where the program was. Its first line usually points at your file, with a line and column number.
options: A list of all the packages you installed
The list of at … lines showing the path the program took to reach the error
The version history saved by Git
A log of every line the program printed

questions.q: Why must a backend catch runtime errors instead of letting them crash the program?
questions.explain: A server answers many people. If one bad request crashed it, everyone would lose the service. With try/catch, the error is handled and the program keeps running.
options: Because errors make the code slower
One bad request must never stop the server for everyone
Because caught errors are sent to the browser to fix
Because catch turns a syntax error into a logic error

The program is still running

questions.explain: You only write what happens for one task: console.log("New task:", title). The framework calls your function once per title.

New task: Buy milk
New task: Write report

questions.q: Use JavaScript's built-in Math library to print the biggest of the numbers 4, 12 and 7, and on the next line 7.6 rounded to the nearest whole number. The output must be 12 and then 8.
questions.explain: Math.max(4, 12, 7) gives 12, and Math.round(7.6) gives 8. You call the library, and use its answers: that is what a library is.

questions.q: Three items cost 5, 15 and 40. Print Total: 60 on the first line and Average: 20 on the second. Watch out for the order of operations.
questions.explain: For the average, the sum must be in brackets: (a + b + c) / 3. Without them, only c is divided by 3 and you get a logic error.
